subject: Anatomy
summary: The facial nerve (CN VII) emerges from the brainstem, loops around the stylomastoid foramen, and supplies muscles of facial expression, taste to the anterior tongue, and glands. Its anatomy explains common palsies and surgical risks.

sections.p: The facial nerve is a mixed cranial nerve with motor, sensory, parasympathetic, and taste fibers. Its complex course makes it vulnerable to trauma, infection, and tumors.
Originates in the pons, joins the abducens nerve, exits the skull via the internal acoustic meatus, traverses the facial canal, and exits the stylomastoid foramen.
Adjacent to the vestibulocochlear nerve, the facial nerve is protected by the temporal bone but can be compressed by cholesteatoma or tumors.
Supplied by the stylomastoid artery (branch of the posterior auricular) and the deep auricular artery.
Motor fibers to facial muscles, parasympathetic fibers to lacrimal, submandibular, and sublingual glands, and taste fibers to the anterior tongue.
b: Parasympathetic to lacrimal and salivary glands

sections.p: Controls facial expression, conveys taste from the anterior tongue, and regulates lacrimal and salivary secretion.
Common injuries include birth trauma, Bell’s palsy, Lyme disease, otitis media, and tumors. Clinical assessment distinguishes UMN vs LMN lesions.
b: Birth forceps injury causes LMN palsy

t.b: Assesses severity of facial weakness; 1 normal, 6 complete paralysis
Detects tumors or cholesteatoma compressing the nerve
Evaluates concurrent hearing loss indicating possible labyrinthine involvement

sections.p: Remember the ‘three‑step’ rule: root, trunk, and branches. LMN lesions spare forehead movement; UMN lesions spare forehead due to bilateral cortical input.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe facial weakness with rapid progression, associated with hearing loss or vertigo, or if there is a facial abscess or suspected tumor.

faq.q: Why does the forehead move in Bell’s palsy?
faq.a: Because the upper facial muscles receive bilateral cortical input, so contralateral cortex can compensate for a unilateral LMN lesion.

faq.q: Can a facial nerve palsy be caused by a stroke?
faq.a: Yes, but only the lower face is affected; the forehead remains intact due to bilateral cortical control.

faq.q: What is the first step in managing a newborn with facial weakness?
faq.a: Assess for birth trauma, rule out infection, and provide supportive care; refer to ENT if cholesteatoma is suspected.

exam: Explain the anatomical course of the facial nerve and why it is vulnerable to birth trauma.
Differentiate between upper motor neuron and lower motor neuron facial palsy based on forehead involvement.
Describe the diagnostic workup for a patient with facial weakness and hearing loss.
